title: How to Choose the Right Car Seat
summary: Choosing a car seat isn't about the priciest option or the most features. A Child Passenger Safety Technicians breaks down the different seat types, when to go infant vs. convertible, and how to know if a seat will fit your car.
body_markdown:
Buying a child car seat is like buying a car—there are many different models and lots of opinions on what’s best. It can feel like a huge decision, particularly for first time parents. After all, what’s at stake is the safety of their baby.


Child Passenger Safety Technicians (CPSTs) are car seat experts, so we know how to navigate the challenges in choosing, installing and using a car seat, and what questions parents and caregivers should ask before they pick a product.


Here, we will explain the three things that really matter in a child seat: the different types, what to look for, and how to choose a car seat that’s right for your child.


- **What Should I Look for When Choosing a Car Seat?**
- **What Are the Different Types of Car Seats?**
- **Should I Start with an Infant Seat or a Convertible Seat?**
- **Should I Buy a New or Used Car Seat?**
- **How Do I Know a Car Seat Will Fit My Vehicle?**
- **Frequently Asked Questions**
- **Bottom Line**


Question Short answer


**What matters most when choosing a car seat?** Once you identify the correct stage of car seat. Then, ensure it fits your child, fits your vehicle, and that you'll install and use it correctly every time.


**Is one type of car seat safer than another?** No — all car seats sold in the U.S. must meet the same federal crash-test standard (FMVSS 213).


**Should I buy an infant seat or a convertible first?** It depends - infant seats are designed specifically for infants and offer portability and stroller click-in; convertibles cost more upfront but they are safe for a larger range of child sizes, meaning you can use them for longer.


**Is it safe to buy a used car seat?** Only if you can verify its full history — otherwise, buy new.


## What Should I Look for When Choosing a Car Seat?


The best car seat is the one that’s designed for your child’s age and size, fits your vehicle, and is one you’ll be able to install and use correctly every single time.


CPSTs like to refer to these three questions when helping people find the right seat for their family.


Does the seat fit the child? The first consideration for parents and caregivers is the seat’s height and weight range. This should be clear from its marketing, packaging, and labelling, but it’s important to focus on the specific height and weight range and not be swayed by the generic recommended age, which is best considered a rough guide.


Does the seat fit the vehicle? Just like cars, seats vary in size and shape, so the two aren’t always going to be a good match. A seat could have phenomenal safety ratings and come highly recommended, but if it doesn’t fit in your car, then it’s not right for you.


Will you use the seat correctly every time? Make sure the car seat has features that help simplify installation. Even the seat with the highest safety rating will fail to protect a child if it is not installed correctly. Correct use includes securing the child in the seat. **[Chicco](https://www.chiccousa.com/)** found that more than 80% of parents use their car seat more than 10 times per week, so prioritize those features that make harnessing and adjusting the seat easy¹.


The Three-Fit Framework


- **Fits the child:** Focus on the seat's specific height and weight range, not the generic recommended age.
- **Fits the vehicle:** A seat with great safety ratings still isn't right for you if it doesn't fit your car.
- **Used correctly every time:** Even the highest-rated seat fails to protect a child if it isn't installed and secured correctly.


This technique is intended to steer shoppers away from questions such as ‘which brand should I buy?’ or ‘how much should I spend?’ and instead direct them towards the most appropriate car seat for them based on their everyday lifestyle. There’s nothing to stop you from considering those factors and others, but the Three-Fit Framework cuts through the noise and prioritizes fitness for purpose above all else.


It also proves that the right seat isn’t necessarily the most expensive one, as all car seats sold in the U.S. must pass the same federal crash-test standard (FMVSS 213) to ensure compliance.


## What Are the Different Types of Car Seats?


There are four core types of car seat: infant, convertible, all-in-one, and booster. Here they are in detail.


Infant seat In general terms, these seats are designed to fit newborns and infants potentially up to 18 months old, but they come with specific usage guidelines.


Infant seats are always rear-facing, because this is the safest riding position for very young children. The typical weight limits are around 30 lbs., and height limits are usually about 30-32 inches. When they’ve grown to a point where their head is within an inch of the top of the seat, it’s time to move onto a bigger model.


Convertible These versatile seats vary by model but are typically meant to grow with the child for stages from newborn through toddlerhood up to the booster phase. They’re a long-lasting option for parents looking to make a purchase that grows with their child. Typically, the weight limits range from 5 – 65 lbs. and the height limits are up to 49 inches.


CPSTs recommend sticking with a rear-facing seat for as long as possible (the height and weight limits of the specific seat should always be your guide, and children usually reach the height limit before the weight limit), because its cradle style is the safest configuration for any baby’s fragile neck and spine in the event of a crash.


Booster These can be either high-backed or backless and are designed for children aged at least four years or older or around 40 lbs. and 44 inches tall. There’s also a maturity factor for the child, as they need to be able to sit relatively still in the same seated position throughout the ride. They represent the last stage in the car seat journey, securing children until an adult seatbelt fits them correctly.


All-in-one As the name suggests, these multi-stage seats transition from rear-facing to forward-facing harness mode and then to a booster seat, providing all stages in one convenient car seat.


Type Orientation Typical stage Best for


**Rear-facing infant seat** Rear-facing only Birth to ~12–18 months Newborns; portable, clicks into a stroller


**Convertible** Rear-facing → forward-facing Birth through preschool years ~6 years (varies by model) Extended rear-facing; stays installed in the vehicle


**All-in-one** Rear-facing → forward-facing → booster Birth through ~10–12 years One seat for the entire journey


**Booster (high-back or backless)** Forward-facing, belt-positioning ~4 years until an adult seat belt fits properly Positioning the adult belt correctly on a bigger kid


## Should I Start with an Infant Seat or a Convertible Seat?


Both infant seats and certain types of convertible seats are suitable for newborn babies. They’re both safe when installed correctly, and there’s no hard and fast rule that says you have to choose one over the other, so this one’s a more subjective question of what works best for you and your family.


Infant seats are the traditional first car seat for newborns and usually chosen over their convertible equivalent because of their portability. Infant seats usually have a base that remains mounted in the car, so the seat can be easily clicked in and out, which offers a number of convenience advantaged.


First, because the car seat can be easily installed or removed from the base, it’s very easy to move a sleeping baby without waking them. It’s also easier to safely secure the infant in the seat, as you can buckle them inside your home before carrying them in the seat out to the car.


Finally, infant seats fit straight into an accompanying stroller. All of these features make infant seats incredibly convenient for parents and caregivers.


However, as the name suggests, children usually outgrow infant seats before 18 months, which means a second seat purchase is in the cards.


Convertible seats lack that click and go flexibility since they don’t have a detachable base, so they stay placed in the car. That said, they streamline additional car seat purchases. If it’s properly cared for, a single convertible seat can see a child from birth through to booster seat age.


Some families find a hybrid approach works best. They might start with an infant seat because they like its convenience during the child’s first year, then graduate to a convertible seat later on to continue their rear-facing goals.


Infant seat / travel system Convertible seat


**Portability** Clicks out of the car; moves a sleeping baby without waking them Stays installed in the vehicle


**Typical lifespan** ~12–18 months before outgrown Several years, often through the preschool stage


**Upfront cost** Usually lower per seat, but a second seat is needed within a year or two Usually higher upfront; one purchase covers that stage


**Best for** Frequent short trips, multiple caregivers/vehicles, stroller click-in Families who prefer to buy once and skip a second purchase


## Should I Buy a New or Used Car Seat?


We get this question a lot. Kids are expensive, and any opportunity to save money is worth investigating, which is why lots of parents and caregivers ask if it’s safe to buy a used car seat.


*Only buy a used or hand-me-down car seat if you can verify its full history—it should never have been in a crash, it should not have expired, it should include all original parts and come with the manual. If you can’t confirm all of that with 100% certainty, buy new.*


Like all degradable materials, car seat strap fibers and plastics gradually break down over time, and everyday wear and tear, exposure to sunlight, temperatures, and fluctuations in humidity have an impact on their longevity. The expiration date can usually be found molded or printed on the seat shell, on a label, or in the owner’s manual. If you are unsure, it is recommended that you buy a new car seat.


Our article **[Car Seat Safety: Mistakes, Expiration Dates, and Care](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/car-seat-safety-mistakes-expiration-dates-and-care)** explains expiration dates in more detail.


## How Do I Know a Car Seat Will Fit My Vehicle?


The majority of car seat manufacturers provide all key measurements of a seat to determine whether it might be a good fit for your vehicle. Use a tape measure to check the width and height available in your car, and if you plan to use the middle seat for your installation, make sure you measure it specifically, as it is often narrower.


There’s also a growing demand for slimmer car seats that would fit three across in a back seat, so if three across is what your family needs, measuring is even more important.


The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) publishes[ease-of-use ratings](https://www.nhtsa.gov/car-seats-and-booster-seats/car-seat-ease-use-ratings) for car seats, which is a great starting point for comparing installation features across different models, so I’d recommend checking that out first


Also, measure to ensure the base of the car seat should sit solidly on the vehicle seat, with no more than a 20% overhang. Take the following factors into consideration when installing as well: which side of the vehicle to install your car seat on, i.e. if the driver needs more leg room, the passenger side is better, or if you park on the street, install on the side closest to the sidewalk.


If you’re not sure whether a particular car seat model will fit your car, contact or visit your local store and ask about test installation before you commit to a purchase. This is particularly worthwhile if your car’s interior is on the tight side or if it has an unusual back seat.


We’ve also published a **[Complete Guide to Car Seat Installation](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/the-complete-guide-to-car-seat-installation)** , so check that out for information.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the safest type of car seat?


Every car seat sold in the U.S. must pass the federal crash-test standard (FMVSS 213). The safest type of car seat is a properly installed seat, which means correct fit, correct installation, and correct stage for your child. Whether buying new or used, visit the[National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) website](https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls) to ensure the car seat model has not been recalled.


### Should I buy an infant seat or go straight to a convertible?


This one’s down to personal preference. Infant seats allow more flexibility, but children typically grow out of them by the time they’re a year and a half. Convertibles cost more and they’re less flexible, but you won’t have to replace them as quickly.


### Is it safe to buy a used car seat?


Only ever consider a used car seat if you can fully verify that it hasn’t been involved in a crash, has not reached its expiry date, and comes with all of its original parts and its owner’s manual. Otherwise, buy new. Make sure to confirm your used car seat has not been recalled by visiting nhtsa.gov. Our article **[Car Seat Safety: Mistakes, Expiration Dates, and Care](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/car-seat-safety-mistakes-expiration-dates-and-care)** has more information.


### Do I need a travel system?


Travel systems are combo products that include an infant car seat, its base, and a compatible stroller. There’s no requirement to use one, but many parents find travel systems practical and convenient since they make it easier to move baby in the infant car seat from the car to the stroller without taking them in and out of the seat. However, if you choose this option, remember to give your baby occasional breaks from reclining in a car seat too long.


### What's the difference between a convertible seat and an all-in-one seat?


Both convertible and all-in-one car seats go from rear-facing to forward-facing harness modes, but all-in-one car seats offer extended use through the booster-seat stage, and can accommodate kids up to110 lbs. and 57 inches tall in booster mode.


### How do I know a car seat will fit my car before I buy it?


Measure your vehicle’s backseat and compare against the specs of the car seat you’re considering. Check if the seat offers features like removable cup-holders or multiple recline settings, which could help improve fit.


## Bottom Line


A good quality car seat is one of the best decisions parents and caregivers can make, but that doesn’t mean the most expensive option or the one with the most high-tech features is right for you.


The right car seat is one that fits the child, fits the car, and will be used correctly every time.


This advice from Chicco and other content on the CarGurus family hub is designed to help consumers understand the ins and outs of car seats. Check out our articles **[The Complete Guide to Car Seat Installation](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/the-complete-guide-to-car-seat-installation)** and **[Car Seat Safety: Mistakes, Expiration Dates, and Care](https://www.cargurus.com/research/articles/car-seat-safety-mistakes-expiration-dates-and-care)** for more, and you can also watch our video Car Seats: How to with the Gurus.
